name: Milk fever

agents.name: Calcium
agents.notes: Not an infectious agent, but a nutrient whose homeostatic control fails at parturition. The disorder is a failure of calcium mobilisation relative to the sudden calcium drain of colostrum and milk production, not a deficiency of calcium in the diet as such.

agents.name: Parturition and onset of lactation
agents.notes: The physiological trigger. The abrupt onset of milk synthesis in a high-producing dairy cow creates a calcium demand that can exceed the ability of the parathyroid hormone and vitamin D axis to mobilise calcium from bone and gut.

hosts.notes: High-producing dairy cows are the classic risk group — older, high-yielding cows in their third or later lactation. Jerseys and Guernseys are more susceptible than Holsteins. Ewes can develop the equivalent disorder in late pregnancy (pregnancy toxaemia-adjacent hypocalcaemia).

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health or trade significance. Its importance is purely economic and welfare-related.

distribution: Worldwide in dairy production systems. Particularly common in high-producing herds where cows are fed high-potassium forage and are not transitioned onto a controlled pre-calving diet.

aetiology.summary: Milk fever results from the failure of calcium homeostasis at the onset of lactation. The cow's calcium demand rises abruptly with colostrum production and milk synthesis, and the parathyroid response — bone resorption, renal conservation and increased intestinal absorption — is too slow to compensate, particularly when the diet is rich in potassium and low in magnesium.
determinants: A sudden increase in calcium demand at parturition and the onset of lactation
Delayed or inadequate parathyroid hormone response and bone calcium mobilisation
High dietary potassium, which reduces the responsiveness of the calcium-regulating mechanism
Low dietary magnesium, which impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and action
Age and lactation number, with older cows having a reduced capacity to mobilise bone calcium
risk_factors: High-producing dairy cows in their third or later lactation
High-potassium forage, such as lush pasture or silage from heavily fertilised land
Low-magnesium diets, particularly in spring grazing
Jersey and Guernsey breeds, which are genetically more susceptible
Sudden onset of high milk yield after calving
Absence of a transition diet or anionic salt programme before calving
aetiology.epidemiology: Milk fever is one of the most common metabolic disorders of dairy cattle, affecting a significant proportion of cows in some herds. Incidence is highest in the first 48 hours after calving. It recurs in subsequent lactations in affected cows and is a risk factor for secondary conditions, including retained placenta, metritis and displaced abomasum.

pathophysiology.summary: The onset of lactation drains calcium into colostrum faster than the parathyroid axis can mobilise it from bone, producing a rapid fall in ionised calcium. Because calcium is required for neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction and cardiac function, the deficiency produces the flaccid paralysis, recumbency and blunted gut and uterine motility that define the syndrome.

cascade.title: Calcium drain at parturition
cascade.detail: Colostrum contains a large amount of calcium, and the start of milk synthesis removes calcium from the extracellular pool abruptly — the demand can exceed the entire extracellular calcium pool within hours.

cascade.title: Impaired parathyroid response
cascade.detail: The parathyroid gland should respond to falling ionised calcium by increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. In a cow with a high-potassium diet, the parathyroid receptor is less responsive, so the response is delayed and inadequate.

cascade.title: Falling ionised calcium
cascade.detail: Ionised calcium, the physiologically active fraction, falls below around 0.8 millimoles per litre. Because calcium is needed for neurotransmitter vesicle release at the neuromuscular junction, this produces a failure of excitation-contraction coupling.

cascade.title: Flaccid paralysis and recumbency
cascade.detail: Muscle tone is lost, producing the characteristic recumbency, and smooth muscle motility is reduced, producing ruminal stasis and a blunted uterine response. The head often rests on the flank, and the animal may become unable to stand.

cascade.title: Cardiac and respiratory compromise
cascade.detail: Cardiac output falls, producing tachycardia and hypotension. Prolonged recumbency adds pressure myopathy and nerve injury, which explains why some cows do not rise even after calcium correction.

lesions: No characteristic gross lesions — the disorder is functional
Evidence of recumbency-related pressure myopathy in the hindlimbs in prolonged cases
Possible concurrent retained placenta, metritis or displaced abomasum
clinical_signs: Recumbency, usually within 48 hours of calving, with the head resting on the flank
Cold extremities and a subnormal temperature
Flaccid paralysis with the animal unable to rise
Dilated pupils and reduced pupillary reflex
Dry muzzle and skin, with reduced sweating
Tachycardia with weak, arrhythmic heart sounds
In mild cases, tremors, ataxia and a wobbly gait before recumbency

antemortem: Clinical diagnosis based on recumbency within 48 hours of calving in a multiparous dairy cow, with no fever
Response to intravenous calcium is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Blood analysis showing low total and ionised calcium
Differentiate from hypomagnesaemia, ketosis and traumatic injury
postmortem: No diagnostic lesion — diagnosis is made clinically
Examine for secondary complications such as displaced abomasum or aspiration pneumonia
laboratory: Serum calcium below 2.0 millimoles per litre, with ionised calcium below 0.8 millimoles per litre in the acute form
Serum magnesium and phosphorus to identify concurrent deficiencies
differentials: Hypomagnesaemia (grass tetany) — similar recumbency but often with tetany, hyperaesthesia and convulsions
Ketosis — recumbency with a ketone smell, reduced appetite and a different response to therapy
Traumatic injury — pelvic fracture or limb fracture after slipping
Displaced abomasum — usually presents with anorexia and reduced milk yield rather than flaccid recumbency
Botulism — flaccid paralysis without the calving-associated timing
Septic metritis — fever and toxaemia distinguish it

prevention: Use a transition diet with a low dietary cation-anion difference (DCAD) before calving to acidify the blood and prime bone calcium mobilisation
Feed low-potassium forage in the close-up dry period
Ensure adequate magnesium in the pre-calving diet
Provide a calcium binder or oral calcium supplementation to high-risk cows around calving
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a metabolic disorder.
treatment: Intravenous calcium borogluconate (usually as a 23% solution) is the specific and life-saving treatment
Administer slowly while monitoring the heart, because rapid infusion can cause arrhythmia and cardiac arrest
Oral calcium supplements, particularly as gels or boluses, for follow-up or for mild cases
Provide bedding and assist the cow to rise; lift her body to allow circulation to recover
Treat secondary complications such as mastitis, metritis or displaced abomasum
Note that a cow that does not rise after calcium is likely to have pressure myopathy or another problem
outbreak: Review the pre-calving diet and transition management
Check forage potassium and magnesium levels
Introduce a DCAD programme under veterinary supervision
Consider oral calcium boluses for all cows around calving in problem herds
Monitor the incidence and identify the at-risk group
public_health: Milk fever has no human health significance
Milk from treated cows is subject to withdrawal periods only if antibiotics or other veterinary medicines have been administered
control.notes: The 'downer cow' is the practical challenge. Calcium corrects the hypocalcaemia within minutes, but an animal that has been recumbent for hours may already have pressure myopathy that no amount of calcium will reverse.

prognosis: Excellent with prompt intravenous calcium — many cows stand within minutes to hours. Guarded if recumbency has been prolonged, because of the risk of pressure myopathy, aspiration pneumonia and secondary conditions.
